patient.chief_complaint: Progressive ascending quadriplegia and bulbar weakness developing on day 2 of hospitalization for head trauma with subarachnoid hemorrhage.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W. is a 72-year-old man with vascular dementia who was brought to the emergency department 2 days ago after a mountain fall. He sustained a head injury with multiple bruising. CT head showed subarachnoid hemorrhage and acute subdural hematoma with bilateral parietooccipital hypodensities. He received a tetanus vaccine. His GCS on admission was 13. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated CK at 20,518 IU/L from crush injury. CT angiography showed no aneurysm or vasospasm. His wounds were treated. On hospital day 2 — which is now — he is developing progressive ascending weakness of all four extremities and is noted to have bulbar weakness with reduced gag. He cannot lift his legs and has marked bilateral upper extremity weakness. Global areflexia is present. His SpO2 has dropped to 93% on room air. This acute ascending neurological deterioration in the context of head trauma creates a challenging differential: central nervous system injury progression, post-traumatic myelopathy, and new neurological complications must be distinguished from GBS. However, GBS can follow trauma as a trigger. The bilateral parietooccipital MRI signal changes likely represent posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) in the context of hypertension and trauma — these do not explain the peripheral areflexia and ascending paralysis, which point to GBS.

critical_actions: Intubate immediately — SpO2 93% with ascending quadriplegia is respiratory failure; do not delay
MRI spine is mandatory to exclude traumatic cord injury before attributing weakness to GBS
CSF protein interpretation is confounded by concurrent SAH — correct for RBCs; elevated protein beyond SAH-expected range supports GBS
Physical trauma is a recognized GBS trigger — the fall preceded the neurological syndrome
PRES (bilateral parietooccipital T2) is a concurrent finding from hypertension — does not explain peripheral areflexia
contraindicated_actions: Succinylcholine for RSI — use rocuronium in GBS
Attributing ascending paralysis to the SAH without NCS/CSF confirmation
key_reasoning_points: Physical trauma (falls, surgery) is a recognized GBS trigger — immune activation from tissue injury can precipitate GBS
PRES in this patient (bilateral parietooccipital T2 changes) is a separate diagnosis from the peripheral neuropathy — two concurrent diagnoses can coexist
CSF in concurrent SAH patients requires careful interpretation — adjust for blood contamination; protein elevated beyond SAH-expected supports GBS
Complete quadriplegia with bulbar weakness on day 2 of hospitalization represents GBS that was already developing at the time of the fall
Seronegative GBS (no ganglioside antibodies) in ~50% of cases — clinical diagnosis based on NCS + CSF
